produced_by.sampler: sizing.mc — inverse transform, Iman-Conover rank correlation

correlations.because: A platform that is growing is a platform that is being changed, and labels arrive with changes. Treating the two as independent makes the metrics interval narrower than the estate warrants — ch14 measures by how much.

Weak and positive: busier services tend to be the chattier ones. Small enough to be worth including as an example of a correlation that barely matters, which is a useful thing for a reader to see beside one that does.

A busier platform is one more people are watching. Moderate rather than strong: most query load comes from alert rules and dashboards on timers, which do not care how busy anything is — right up until an incident, when they all fire at once and nobody is looking at the model.

summary.description:
The book's sizing exemplar, and the counterweight to the storage cluster. Three multiplicative chains hang off the same few roots, so they are correlated whether or not anybody says so; label cardinality is a product of uncertain counts and therefore dominates everything downstream of it; the control knobs are sampling and retention rather than money; and there are three separate outputs with three separate ceilings, which no single number can summarise.
It also has a hole in it. Spans per request is a property of somebody's instrumented application, not of any corpus or any machine, so this repository cannot measure it — and the whole traces chain is therefore shown as unmeasured rather than filled in with a plausible number. That is not a gap waiting to be tidied up. It is what an honest sizing model looks like before the measurement is taken, and it is on a published page for exactly that reason.

known_ingest.note: Metrics plus logs, and deliberately *not* the total. It is a lower bound with a whole chain missing from it, and ch19 is about exactly this shape of error: a number that is correct arithmetic over an incomplete structure looks identical to a number that is right.

known_storage_cost.label: retention cost, metrics and logs only

label_cardinality.label: label cardinality
label_cardinality.note: A product of uncertain counts, which is why it is lognormal-ish whether or not anybody chose that, and why it dominates the tornado for every metrics figure in this model. Multiplying three quantities that are each uncertain by a factor of three gives one uncertain by a factor of twenty-seven, and no amount of care about the other inputs recovers that.

label_values_accidental.label: accidental label values
label_values_accidental.note: The label nobody planned. A pod name under a rolling deploy, a customer id added during an incident, a version string. Lognormal and wide, because the failure mode is multiplicative: whatever it is, it multiplies every series that carries it, and the distribution has to be able to express "usually nothing, occasionally catastrophic".

ceiling.because: Queueing again, and the tier where a breach is most visible: a dashboard that times out during an incident is the failure people remember. Cardinality feeds this and the ingest ceiling by different routes, so a single accidental label breaks both at once.

A queueing ceiling, not a capacity one (ch06), so the margin is large: a pipeline at 80% of quoted throughput has a queue in front of it, and a queue in front of an ingest pipeline is dropped telemetry exactly when something is going wrong. Understated twice over — the numerator excludes traces and the denominator is a vendor's claim.

series_per_query.label: series per query
series_per_query.note: The same cardinality node that drives the metrics ingest chain drives this one too, by a different route: a label that multiplies the series a scrape produces also multiplies the series a query has to walk past to ignore. That is why one accidental label breaks two ceilings at once, and why turning down scrape interval and retention — which fix the first — does nothing at all for the second (ch12).

spans_per_request.note: Not measurable from anything in this repository. It is a property of one instrumented application at one version, so it belongs to the `estate` target — an observation somebody takes of a system they run, disclosed rather than verified (ch03). Until somebody takes it, every figure below is absent rather than estimated.

scenario.because: The same estate with every control knob moved: 60-second scrapes, 90-day metric retention, a tenth of the log lines kept, and 1% trace sampling. Here so that ch12 can put a number on what each knob buys — and so the reader can see that the knobs do not touch cardinality at all, which is the input that dominates everything.
